name: Question 4
problem:
Consider the following boundary value problem (BVP).

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+3y=0,\,y(1)={y}^{′}(3)=0,\,1\le x\le 3
$$

Let ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ be the fundamental solutions, and suppose we define the matrix $A$ as 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(3) & {y}_{2}^{′}(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

Fill in the correct options in the reasoning below.

$\,$ The boundary value problem has a unique solution if and only if {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The fundamental solutions to this BVP are {{field-2}}.

$\,$ For this BVP, we have $det(A)=$ {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Therefore, this BVP {{field-4}}.
worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}(x)+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0,
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$   

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Robin boundary conditions given by

$$
y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(3)=0.
$$

So, setting ${\alpha }_{1}=1,$ ${\beta }_{1}=0,$ ${\alpha }_{2}=0,$ ${\beta }_{2}=1,$ and $a=1,$ $b=3,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(3) & {y}_{2}^{′}(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-4m+3 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have ${m}_{1}=1$ and ${m}_{2}=3,$ and so the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\,\text{and}\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=3{e}^{3x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{1} & {e}^{3(1)} \\ {e}^{3} & 3{e}^{3(3)}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}e & {e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & 3{e}^{9}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =e(3{e}^{9})-{e}^{3}({e}^{3}) \\  & =3{e}^{10}-{e}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6}(3{e}^{4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

y″(x)+P(x)y′(x)+Q(x)y=0,a≤x≤b

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

α1y(a)+β1y′(a)=0,α2y(b)+β2y′(b)=0, where P and Q are continuous on [a,b], and αi,βi are real constants such that (αi,βi)≠(0,0). Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are y1(x) and y2(x).

Now, let's define the following matrix:

A=[α1y1(a)+β1y1′(a)α1y2(a)+β1y2′(a)α2y1(b)+β2y1′(b)α2y2(b)+β2y2′(b)].

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution y≡0 if and only if det(A)≠0.
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that, in our case, we have Robin boundary conditions given by
y(1)=0,y′(3)=0. So, setting α1=1, β1=0, α2=0, β2=1, and a=1, b=3, the matrix A reduces to

A=[y1(1)y2(1)y1′(3)y2′(3)].

To find the fundamental solutions, we set y=emx. The auxiliary equation is m2−4m+3=0(m−1)(m−3)=0. So, we have m1=1 and m2=3, and so the fundamental solutions are
y1(x)=exandy2(x)=e3x.

Differentiating, we have y1′(x)=ex,y2′(x)=3e3x.

Therefore, the matrix A is

A=[e1e3(1)e33e3(3)]=[ee3e33e9],

and we have det(A)=e(3e9)−e3(e3)=3e10−e6=e6(3e4−1).

Since det(A)≠0, we conclude that this BVP has the unique solution y≡0.
